At 03:14 in the morning, the universe narrows to the diameter of a single vacuum tube. 

Inside the small octagonal room at the tip of Point Disappointment, the glass bulb glows with an amber filament no thicker than a horsehair. It smells of hot dust, varnished teak, and the iron-sharp tang of sea spray blown through the window casements. Outside, the Pacific does what it has done for three million years: it throws itself against black basalt until the basalt turns to sand, and the sand turns into memory.

My title on the government ledger is *Station Monitor, Grade III*, but titles are just small cages built to hold large emptinesses. What I actually do is listen to the spaces between things.

The console before me is a relic of late-twentieth-century optimism, constructed from cold-rolled steel and enameled in battleship gray. It is equipped with fifty-four knurled aluminum dials, three phosphor-green oscilloscopes that draw slow, luminous green ribbons across the dark, and an array of magnetic tape reels that turn with the languid, deliberate grace of deep-sea creatures. 

The world assumes that radio is a medium of voices—of weather warnings, maritime distress, pop songs compressed into bright three-minute candies, and the frantic urgency of news anchors announcing disasters that have already occurred. But if you dial down below the commercial bands, down past the amateur operators chattering about antenna gain in drafty basements, down into the long-wave cellar of the spectrum between thirty and sixty kilohertz, the human voice ceases to exist.

Down here, there is only the geology of the ionosphere.

If you tune the receiver to 44.2 kHz on a night like this, when a low-pressure front is grinding its teeth against the coastal range, you do not hear silence. Silence is a fiction invented by people who have never sat in a room without a clock. Instead, you hear the solar wind raking its fingers through the upper atmosphere. You hear the electromagnetic shriek of lightning strikes occurring six thousand miles away in the Congo Basin, their signals bounced around the curvature of the earth between the ground and the sky, arriving here as thin, glassy pops—like someone walking in heavy boots across a floor of frozen leaves.

You hear the ghosts of meteors. When a grain of space dust the size of a mustard seed strikes the mesosphere at forty miles per second, it burns into a brief, incandescent trail of ionized gas. For half a second, that scar in the sky acts as a mirror for stray television signals from forgotten transmitters in Idaho or Hokkaido. A fragment of a late-night weather report from 1984 will bounce off that fleeting scar and land in my headphones: *"...highs tomorrow near sixty-eight with a slight chance of..."*—and then the sky mends itself, and the voice vanishes back into the static.

I keep a logbook bound in black buckram. The pages are ruled in pale blue gridlines. 

*Entry 1,402:* 02:22 UTC. Atmospheric ducting over the Juan de Fuca Strait. Carrier wave detected on 5,125 kHz. No modulation. Steady as a heartbeat. Duration: eleven minutes.

*Entry 1,403:* 03:05 UTC. Whistler event. Descending tone from 8 kHz to 400 Hz. Resembles the sigh of an animal entering deep water.

People often ask why a man would choose to live on a spit of rock thirty miles from the nearest grocery store, with only two hundred gulls and a diesel generator for company. They think it must be grief. They imagine a lost love, a ruinous bankruptcy, or some unspoken crime of youth that drove me into exile. 

Humans love the architecture of tragedy; it gives isolation a reason. But the truth is simpler and far less romantic: I like things that do not demand to be answered.

In the cities, every sound is an invoice. A car horn demands your panic; a phone chime demands your attention; a billboard demands your desire; a conversation demands your agreement or your defense. Everything is an exchange of currencies you never agreed to trade.

Here, the static demands nothing. The long-wave hum does not care if I am listening. It was singing its low, mechanical hymn when the coastline was buried under two miles of Pleistocene ice, and it will be singing it when the steel console before me has dissolved into a red crust of oxide. There is an immense, almost holy mercy in being entirely irrelevant to the thing you are observing.

At 04:00, the tea in my enamel mug has gone the temperature of river stones. I leave the headphones around my neck—where they murmur like a pair of dry shells held to the ears—and step out onto the gallery deck.

The fog has arrived. It does not roll in; it accumulates, condensing out of the dark until the light from the lantern overhead cannot push more than ten feet into the murk. The beam of the lighthouse swings through the white smother, a solid spoke of yellow light turning endlessly through grease.

Down below, the bell buoy at the reef groans on the swell. *Clang. Clang.* A heavy, unhurried bronze syllable that marks the rise and fall of the planet’s breath. 

I lean against the cold rail and watch the light sweep past. For a fraction of a second, the fog is illuminated from within, like an opal held to a candle, revealing the trillion individual droplets suspended in the air, each one reflecting the lantern, each one an eye that opens and closes in the turn of a gear.

We spend our lives waiting for profound signals. We wait for the letter that explains why we were not enough, the diagnosis that explains our fatigue, the voice from the clouds that tells us which fork in the road to take. We wait for an alien intelligence to beam prime numbers from the vicinity of Tau Ceti, or for the dead to knock twice on the underside of the table.

We ignore the noise that fills the room while we wait. We ignore the slow friction of tectonic plates sliding past each other in the dark, the faint hiss of the radiator bleeding air, the sound of our own pulse beating against the bone of the inner ear.

Back inside, the amber tube continues to glow. The needle on the signal-strength meter twitches—just once, a slight shudder to the right, as if nudged by a passing thought—and then settles back into the baseline.

I pick up my fountain pen. The black ink pools on the nib, wet and glossy in the lamp-glow.

*Entry 1,404:* 04:18 UTC. Sea fog thick. Sky quiet. All frequencies clear.

I close the book, blow out the desk lamp, and let the room fill with the sound of the ocean, which is only another kind of static, waiting for no one.
